relations.note: Latvian songs repeatedly identify the divine horsemen as Dievs’s sons.

relations.myth: Celestial wedding and neighboring heavenly households
relations.note: Their heavenly households are allied through his sons’ courtship of Saule’s daughters.

relations.myth: Wedding of Dievs’s sons and Saule’s daughters
relations.note: Mēness exchanges rings during the celestial wedding involving Dievs’s sons.

relations.myth: Celestial wedding and striking the golden oak
relations.note: Pērkons joins or disrupts wedding cycles involving Dievs’s sons.

relations.myth: Divine transport in celestial wedding arrangements
relations.note: Variants associate Dievs’s horses and Laima’s wagon with wedding arrangements.

relations.myth: Beneficent invocation with Māra and Laima
relations.note: Traditional formulas jointly invoke Dievs, Māra, and Laima as beneficent powers.
Dievturi theology and art coordinate Dievs with Māra and Laima.

relations.myth: God and Devil create the world
relations.note: They form land, animals, or terrain while Velns imitates or sabotages Dievs.

relations.myth: God and Devil travel among humans
relations.note: They travel together as opposing figures testing hospitality, greed, and disorder.
Christian translators adopted Dievas, Dievs, and Deiws as the ordinary name for God.
Later interpreters equated Łasicki’s highest Samogitian god with Dievas.
Later scholars identified the Sudovian chief god of sky and stars with Dievas.
Later interpreters equated Stryjkowski’s disputed creator or highest deity with Dievas.
Early-modern writers interpreted Baltic supreme or celestial beings through Zeus.
Early-modern writers interpreted Baltic supreme or celestial beings through Jupiter.
